title: The World of AI: AI Courses catalogue in Research and Learning
answer: The World of AI publishes this AI Courses catalogue within its Research and Learning section. It lists 13 AI courses, 11 free, 3 with public companion code, curated by level and audience with one verified source each and reverified daily. Its most useful point is the split between four university graduate courses with public materials and industry courses described as code first or hands on. That makes the choice about how someone wants to learn, not which source is more rigorous. The text also says ten courses in places, so the count is inconsistent.

sections.body: The World of AI publishes this page, titled AI Courses, as part of its AI Research and Learning section. It is a catalogue of courses, not a report or study. It says it tracks 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, curated by level and audience with one verified source each. The page was last verified on 2026-09-29, and source links are re-verified daily. It states that membership is editorial, based on significance rather than sponsorship, and that nothing is paid placement.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page lists courses from DeepLearning.AI on Coursera, Dataquest, fast.ai, and DeepLearning.AI with Stanford on Coursera. It gives level, intended audience, cost, and verification dates for several entries. DeepLearning.AI has a beginner course for managers, executives, and anyone working alongside technical teams, free to audit with a certificate fee listed on the page. Another DeepLearning.AI course is intermediate and intended for after the ML Specialization, also free to audit with a paid certificate. Dataquest is beginner level for developers who want hands on practice with LLM APIs and costs a subscription listed on the page. fast.ai is beginner to intermediate for programmers and top down learners, free, with companion code. A DeepLearning.AI and Stanford course is beginner level, described as the first course for most people, free to audit with a paid certificate. The page says all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials, though three pair that with a paid certificate option or public code repositories. It says four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley CS285, and MIT 6.S191, while the rest come from industry. It argues university courses are generally structured around exam driven theory, while industry courses are code first or hands on, so the choice is about how someone wants to learn rather than which source is more rigorous. Only three courses list an accompanying public code repository, fast.ai, Karpathy's Zero to Hero, and MIT 6.S191.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states 13 AI courses, 11 free, and 3 with public companion code. It also says all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials, which conflicts with the 13 figure. It names four university graduate courses with public materials: Stanford CS224n, Stanford CS231n, UC Berkeley CS285, and MIT 6.S191. It says only three courses list public code repositories: fast.ai, Karpathy's Zero to Hero, and MIT 6.S191. It gives costs as free to audit with certificate fees, paid certificate, subscription, or free. It says last verified 2026-09-29, with source links re-verified daily, and individual course verifications dated 2026-09-28. It states membership is editorial, not paid placement. It does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in Education can use this source as a catalogue of AI courses, with levels, audiences, costs, and code availability. It helps compare university graduate courses, which the source describes as exam driven theory, with industry courses, which it describes as code first or hands on. It also identifies free access to core materials and maps skills to the AI Skills Graph. It is useful for choosing a learning path or for seeing what course providers are tracked, but it is not evidence about learning outcomes or adoption.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Education

sections.body: The source does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken. It is a catalogue page, not a study, and its counts are inconsistent, since it says 13 courses but later refers to ten. It covers only a small set of courses and does not address K-12 education, institutional adoption, policy, or assessment. It is published by The World of AI and includes promotional mentions of books and consulting services, so it has a commercial context. It is dated 2026-09-29 and says links are re-verified daily, but course details and costs can change.
